grounded_facts: Neary mocks Alice’s presence at the weigh-in, calling her an old lady and questioning her place there.
memories.memory_text: I heard Neary mock Alice, asking why an old lady was up there and saying it wasn’t her place, and it made me uneasy seeing her targeted like that.

grounded_facts: The main event at Olympia Grand Hall where Micky Ward faces Shea Neary for the WBU Light Welterweight Title.
memories.memory_text: I saw the crowd pour into the Olympia Grand Hall for Micky's WBU title fight with Shea Neary.

grounded_facts: Dicky questions Sal’s role and competence, demanding to know where the entrance music is.

grounded_facts: Neary refuses to touch gloves with Micky before the fight, instead pressing his forehead aggressively into Micky's as a sign of disrespect.

grounded_facts: Charlene yells at Sal to bring the stool for Micky after he returns to the corner badly hurt at the end of round one.
memories.memory_text: I saw Charlene screaming at Sal to give Micky the stool when he came back to the corner hurt after the first round.

grounded_facts: Dicky delivers an intense emotional speech to Micky during the corner break, urging him not to waste their shared struggle and to channel pain into action.
memories.memory_text: I looked Micky in the eyes and told him not to take unnecessary punishment, that he's not a punchin' bag, and that we've been waitin' our whole lives for this moment — I urged him to take all the emotion and pain from everything we've been through and use it right then.

grounded_facts: Before the third round, Dicky places his forehead against Micky's in a silent, intense moment of brotherly connection and mutual resolve.
memories.memory_text: I took Micky's neck in my hands and pressed my forehead to his, closing my eyes for a moment — I wanted him to feel my presence and know we were in this together, just before the bell rang for the next round.

grounded_facts: Micky survives a brutal first round where Neary overwhelms him with body shots, leaving Micky hurt and unsteady, barely saved by the bell.
memories.memory_text: I saw Micky get hammered in the first round—Neary came out fast, drilling him with body shots, and I watched my brother stagger, barely staying on his feet until the bell saved him.

grounded_facts: After being hurt in round one, Micky regains his composure and legs in round two, beginning to land effective counters and withstand Neary's pressure.
memories.memory_text: I saw Micky hurt in the first round, so I pushed him to jump with me to get his legs back, yelling that he’s not a punchin’ bag and to use all the pain we’ve been through—then I watched him start bouncing on his toes and walk toward Neary, trading punches toe-to-toe like he found his fire again.

grounded_facts: Dicky shouts from ringside, urging Micky to fight his way out of being trapped on the ropes.

memories.memory_text: I saw Micky land that big uppercut and drop Neary—first time in 22 fights he's been knocked down, I heard someone shout it, and I knew right then that everything had changed in that ring.

grounded_facts: Micky hugs Dicky's head between his gloves and laughs, acknowledging his brother's role in the victory.
memories.memory_text: I felt Micky hug my head between his gloves and laugh, and in that moment I knew he recognized how much I’d done for him.

grounded_facts: Dicky jumps into the ring and lifts Micky in the air, expressing overwhelming pride and emotional release.
memories.memory_text: I jumped into the ring and lifted my brother up in my arms, overwhelmed with pride and emotion after everything we'd been through.

grounded_facts: Alice enters the ring and proclaims both Micky and Dicky as champions, affirming her pride in both sons.
memories.memory_text: I was in the ring when my mother came in and said both me and Micky were champions, and I felt her pride in me for the first time in a long while.

grounded_facts: After hugging Micky, Alice turns to Dicky and lovingly fixes the collar of his blood-stained jacket.
memories.memory_text: After she hugged Micky, I saw my mother turn to me and gently fix the collar of my jacket, which was stained with Micky's blood, and it meant everything.

I switched stances, worked my right, then hit him with my left. That punch—it was mine. I knew in that moment I could win, and I did.

grounded_facts: Micky executes a decisive body shot and combination that drops Sanchez to the canvas, leading to a knockout victory.
memories.memory_text: I saw Dicky’s advice play out in front of me like dance steps on the canvas, so I moved inside, switched stances, worked my right, and landed my left—the punch I own—and when Sanchez went down, I knew I had done it.

memories.memory_text: I remember landing that final hook, seeing Neary go down, and hearing the crowd erupt—I knew I’d won the championship.

grounded_facts: The referee stops the fight after Neary's second knockdown, making Micky Ward the new WBU Light Welterweight champion.
memories.memory_text: I saw the referee wave it's over, and when I heard the call that I'd done it, I threw my hands in the air—blood dripping down my face—I knew I was the new WBU Light Welterweight champion.

grounded_facts: Micky hugs Dicky's head between his gloves and laughs, acknowledging his brother's role in the victory.
memories.memory_text: I hugged Dicky's head between my gloves and laughed, calling out 'Dickyeeee!' to let him know how much this victory meant to me and how grateful I was for him.

grounded_facts: Dicky jumps into the ring and lifts Micky in the air, expressing overwhelming pride and emotional release.
memories.memory_text: I felt Dicky jump into the ring and lift me up, holding me in his arms with so much pride—I could see it in his eyes and feel it in his grip.

grounded_facts: Alice enters the ring and proclaims both Micky and Dicky as champions, affirming her pride in both sons.
memories.memory_text: I saw my mother Alice step into the ring and beam at me, then she proclaimed both me and Dicky as champions, saying she loved me and that I was a champion.

grounded_facts: Charlene pulls Micky toward her and kisses him deeply, marking their shared triumph and emotional culmination.
memories.memory_text: I felt Charlene pull me toward her and kiss me deeply, her hands on my face, sealing our triumph in that moment.

grounded_facts: After hugging Micky, Alice turns to Dicky and lovingly fixes the collar of his blood-stained jacket.
memories.memory_text: After hugging me, my mother turned to Dicky and gently fixed the collar of his blood-stained jacket, showing her love for him too.

memories.memory_text: I pounded on Micky's door until he answered, and when he finally opened up, I saw his face all messed up with bandages—I asked him straight why he didn't call me yesterday, then called him out for standing me up after the fight.

I saw the bandage peeling off the left side of his face, pointed it out, asked if he had tape, then made him sit down in the bathroom while I re-did the wrap—my hands were on his skin, fixing it careful, quiet-like, while I asked if that Jewish black guy was the one who hurt him.
I sat there watching the movie, but I couldn't stop looking at Micky—his head was tipped back, mouth hanging open, just out cold while the film played.
I looked at him and said, 'You afraid to run into your girlfriend?' because he was acting so weird, rushing off, not even knowing the keys were in his hand.
He turned the car off and just sat there, then said he came to Lexington because he didn't want to show his face back home—I remember how quiet it got after that.
I ran and jumped backward over that bamboo bar Micky and his kid were holding, cleared 5'1" easy, but those old pillows barely softened the fall—I felt every inch when I landed on my ass.
I told them I was quitting the bar to go for teacher certification, and when Alice smirked and said I was planning to live off Micky, I shot back that she’s been living off him for years.
I don’t remember standing up, but suddenly I was right between Micky and the cops, arms out—I had to block them before they touched him.

I ran out just as Micky stopped on the stairs, and when he said he wanted to meet that guy from George, I nodded—then watched him walk away from the edge of the porch, not moving till I saw him clear.
I stood there with Micky's new team, watching him train, making it clear I was part of this now — no more Alice running his life.
When Alice started throwing things and chaos broke out, I braced myself — I knew it wasn’t over, not with her trying to control everything again.
I stood there in the gym and told Micky straight—'They have to go, Micky'—because I knew Dicky was dragging him down, and I couldn't let him betray O'Keefe like that.
After Micky said he wouldn't have won without Dicky, I screamed 'We saved him! Dickya junkbag!'—I couldn't believe he'd throw us under the bus like that, and I knew nothing was gonna change.

Dicky showed up at my door, sweating and desperate, saying he’d quit using if it meant I’d stay with Micky — I told him he was full of shit, but he just stood there, pushing the buzzer like he actually cared.
He actually paused when I threw his loss in his face, then turned it around — said I didn’t know what it was like to be in that ring, asked what I’d ever done, like my life was just as broken as his.

memories.memory_text: I was high, making out with Karen, and then Wolfie yelled Ma was outside—I panicked, didn't want her to see me like that, so I jumped out the second-floor window and landed hard on garbage bags in the alley.
Micky found me in the alley, and I whispered for him to pick me up at the house later—I couldn't go with him now, not with Ma out front, even though he said we had to go to the airport for the fight.
I grabbed Micky by the shoulders and told him ESPN screwed us, they owe us another fight — he didn’t have to end it like this, he just needed to heal up.
I remember yelling, 'What do you know about anything!' when that Charlene woman brought up the crack house, like she had any right to judge me in front of my family.
I stood outside that crack house, speaking in broken Cambodian, telling them to put in $200 and bring ten more people — I could see the hope and confusion in their eyes.
They started yelling, saying I ripped them off, but I was trying to give them a chance. I love Cambodian people — Karen was right there. I needed to find money for Micky.
I was talking to the camera, trying to explain about Sugar Ray and the money we lost, but my head was spinning—I just needed them to understand it was all for Micky, even if I was high.
I was handling Micky's training, and I know Charlene doubted me, saying Alice would be better than me.

I pulled up behind the Volvo with my brights on and used the megaphone to say, 'Get outta the cah, hands on the roof!' I told him to empty his pockets, took the cash, and told Karen to take half and get us some rocks.
I heard the siren, then that bald guy screaming, 'THAT'S THE GUY!'—I didn't wait, just took off running, sprinting through backyards, heart pounding, knowing the cops were after me now.
I was supposed to meet Micky and the others at the restaurant, but I never made it—something went bad outside, loud voices, then fists, me swinging at the bouncer, cops piling on.
I remember shouting, 'Help! Micky! Somebody!' while they had me down, hands behind my back, cuffed, pain in my face—I needed him and he wasn’t there.
I was playing with my son, just laughin’ with him, and for a second, it felt normal.
Then I heard people sayin’ the HBO thing made the city look bad, that me and Micky were bad for Lowell—that the dream was dead—and I didn’t know what to believe, but it hit me hard.
I had to get back to the house, I told Harry I needed to tell young Dicky it’s gonna be okay—he don’t gotta cry no more. I couldn’t let him sit there scared and alone.
I walked into the dark kitchen on the second floor and sank to my knees on the cement floor, bowing my head.

I was runnin’ the track, soaked in sweat, just tryin’ to stay sharp, and then I heard my name over the loudspeaker—visit from Micky. I sat down across from him, and he told me straight: he’s got new management, O’Keefe and some guy Sal, and it’s goin’ good. No mention of me bein’ in his corner.
I walked in and heard O'Keefe say I couldn't work with Micky anymore — like I don't matter — and I snapped, yelling that Micky never would’ve beaten Sanchez without me.

Micky finally said it — right in front of everyone — that he wouldn't have beaten Sanchez without me, but then they still made me leave, so I walked out knowing I mattered, even if they didn't want me there.
I stood on her porch, sweating, and told Charlene I'd quit—swore to God I'd quit—if it meant Micky could keep her. Micky deserves his shot, not to lose her 'cause of me.
After she yelled at me, I just said 'I'm good' when she asked if I wanted a ride home. I didn't need her pity. I walked away, even though every part of me wanted to run back to the house.

memories.memory_text: I just wanted to say hi to Kasie, but Laurie shut the door in my face, not even letting me have that.
I promised Kasie I'd start making good money and move to a bigger apartment so she could stay with me more, but Laurie laughed and called it cruel.

I saw Dicky flying out that window, crashing into the garbage bags, then struggling to get up like nothing was wrong. I had to help him over the fence while Ma was out front, and all he kept whispering was 'Don't tell Ma.'

George came charging at us, furious, and threw a punch at Dicky. Dicky slipped it and knocked him out with one shot. I just rolled my eyes—there was no time for this, not today, not before the flight.
I stood by the car, just nodding when Dicky said we’d get another fight, but I didn’t believe it. After losing, I told Ma I didn’t wanna do this no more.

I sat up in the dark, took pills, opened a beer, and stared at that napkin with Charlene’s number and the heart drawn on it. I started to call her, then stopped—just put it down and went back to the couch.
I must’ve dozed off in the theater, head back, not aware of anything—just the hum of the movie pulling me under.
I told everyone I was gonna win that fight and get back on track, told Kasie we'd get a bigger place—now I can't even show my face in Lowell.
I didn't say anything—just turned off the car, then leaned in and kissed Charlene, and it wasn't soft or quick, it was like I needed her to know something real.
I told Charlene Dicky's handling it, even though she didn't believe me — I could hear the doubt in her voice, arms crossed like I was wasting her time.

I held one end of the bamboo stick while Kasie held the other, and we watched Charlene leap backward over it — she landed hard on the pillows, rubbing her ass, and I clapped with Kasie like it was a real win.
I walked in, kissed Ma hello, sat down—she was holdin’ up the poster, all proud, askin’ what I thought. I told her it looked great, just like she wanted to hear.
I asked if we could just talk about the fight, tried to keep it focused—everyone else kept draggin’ in the same old stuff, like it was ever really about me.
I ran into Dunkin’ Donuts out of the rain, tired and sore, and suddenly everyone was staring, whispering like I was some kind of joke.
I saw Mickey O’Keefe in uniform, tried to say hey, but I could feel all those eyes still on me, like I couldn’t even breathe right.

I was on the phone with Ma, watching that HBO documentary, and when I opened the door and saw Charlene standing there, I just broke—couldn't hold it in, cried into her shoulder like I hadn't in years.
Next morning, I reached into the dark closet, grabbed the old white wraps and red gloves, tossed them into the blue gym bag—didn't say a word, just knew it was time to go back.
I paused on the stairs and told Charlene I wanted to meet that guy George mentioned—the one with the cab company. Then I walked away, knowing she was watching from the balcony.

I was jumpin' rope, breathin' hard, and saw Sal LoNano watchin' with Charlene and George — I stopped, caught my breath, kissed Charlene, then shook his hand. He said he already made calls for a local fight to get my confidence back.
